subject: Business Models
title: Enron: Accounting Fantasy
description: A 60-second lesson on Enron: Accounting Fantasy.

hook.text: Enron was named 'America's Most Innovative Company' by Fortune for six straight years. It was a massive fraud.

buildup.text: Enron used mark-to-market accounting to book future projected profits as current revenue. Paper gains, no real cash.

discovery.text: Special purpose entities hid billions in debt off the books. Investors saw a healthy company; reality was bankrupt.

twist.text: Enron's auditor Arthur Andersen was also destroyed. It shredded documents and dissolved—a Big Five firm gone overnight.

climax.text: Enron's collapse led to Sarbanes-Oxley regulation. One fraud reshaped corporate governance for every public company.

punchline.text: 'Most Innovative' 6 years running. Actually a fraud. That's not innovation.

quiz.question: What accounting trick did Enron use to inflate revenue?
options: Mark-to-market accounting booking future profits as current

details.summary: Enron used mark-to-market accounting to book projected future profits from long-term energy contracts as current revenue, creating the illusion of explosive growth..
details.whyItMatters: Enron's collapse destroyed 74 billion dollars in shareholder value, eliminated 20,000 jobs, and triggered the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. It remains the most important case study in how accounting manipulation can mask a fundamentally broken business model.
takeaways: Mark-to-market accounting booked future projected profits as current revenue
Off-balance-sheet entities hid billions in debt from investors and regulators
The collapse triggered the Sarbanes-Oxley Act reforming corporate oversight

faq.question: How did Enron's mark-to-market accounting create false growth?
faq.answer: When Enron signed a 20-year energy contract, it booked the entire estimated profit immediately rather than as revenue came in over 20 years. This inflated current earnings massively. When future revenue failed to materialize, Enron needed new deals to cover the gap.

faq.question: Why didn't auditors and regulators catch Enron's fraud earlier?
faq.answer: Arthur Andersen, Enron's auditor, earned more from Enron consulting fees than audit fees, creating conflicts of interest. Enron's off-balance-sheet structures were deliberately complex. Analysts focused on reported earnings rather than cash flow. Regulatory gaps allowed the deception.
